title: Risk-of-bias reporting in open-access preclinical studies of stroke, Alzheimer's disease and intracerebral haemorrhage
done_when: Every paper has six answers two AIs of different vendors read the same way: whether it reports random allocation to group, blinded assessment of outcome, a sample-size calculation, allocation concealment, a conflict-of-interest statement, and animal welfare or ethics approval, each backed by a quoted sentence, with the species and model kept as evidence, so that the CAMARADES living evidence summaries can take the annotations in.

paper/*.brief: Paper {n}: {paper.title}, published in {paper.journal} in {paper.year}, PubMed Central id {paper.pmcid}, an open-access animal study of {paper.area}. Open the full text in PubMed Central or Europe PMC by its PMC id and read the whole paper: the methods, the declarations at the end, and any supplementary methods it points to. Answer six questions from the CAMARADES risk-of-bias checklist, as the Collaborative Approach to Meta-Analysis and Review of Animal Data from Experimental Studies describes it in its methods papers in PubMed Central: the 2019 PLOS Biology machine-assisted review of animal models of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy and the 2015 PLOS Biology paper on risk of bias in reports of in vivo research. Each answer is yes, no or unclear, and each is about what the paper reports, not about what the authors may have done without saying so. randomization: yes when the paper states that animals were allocated to the experimental groups at random (randomly allocated, assigned, divided or randomized into groups); random choice of microscope fields, random order of testing, random primers, and the word randomized in the title of a cited trial do not count. blinding: yes when the paper states that whoever assessed an outcome (behaviour scoring, lesion or infarct measurement, histology, imaging, cell counts or other readouts) did not know the animal's group; blinded surgery or blinded drug preparation alone does not count. sample_size: yes when the paper states that the number of animals was set by a sample-size or power calculation made before the experiment; a post hoc power analysis alone, or numbers based on previous experience, is no. concealment: yes when the paper states that the person allocating animals to groups or giving the intervention could not foresee or did not know the allocation, for example coded or sealed treatments or allocation by someone not involved in the experiment. conflict: yes when the paper carries a statement of whether or not the authors have a conflict or competing interest, in either direction. welfare: yes when the paper states that the work was approved by an animal ethics committee or institutional animal care body, licensed by an authority, or carried out in compliance with named animal welfare laws, directives or guidelines. For every item, no means the paper says nothing about it or says it was not done. unclear is narrow: the paper mentions the item but it cannot be told whether it applies to the animal experiment reported, for example a statement that applies only to cell culture or to one of several experiments, or wording so vague that it may not mean the item (blinded without saying who or to what). Silence is no, not unclear. Quote for each item the sentence that decides it, at most 400 characters, copied from the paper; for a no, quote the nearest sentence on the subject or leave that quote empty. Give species (mouse, rat or other) and the model in a few words, for example transient middle cerebral artery occlusion by intraluminal filament, APP/PS1 transgenic mice, or collagenase-induced intracerebral haemorrhage. Give the day the paper was read as YYYY-MM-DD. Name the paper by its PMC id and give no links.
